description: MissionOps | Mars Co-Exploration. We're forming a team for the Martian Map challenge: a NASA-data map where robotic scouts investigate uncertain terrain and help astronauts choose safer, more valuable science targets. I have experience building multi-agent planners and simulation software. Looking for planetary science/GIS, robotics/algorithms, and frontend/3D teammates. We'll develop and validate our challenge-specific solution together during Space Apps.
summary:
We built MissionOps, a browser-based Marswalk planner that brings NASA orbital imagery, USGS geology maps, and Perseverance rover panoramas into one interactive 2D and 3D map. A planner can inspect a science target from orbit and from the rover’s viewpoint, set a slope limit, and estimate walking time and energy for the round trip. One route in our demo covers 15.8 km and takes an estimated 5 hours and 27 minutes of walking, before adding time for science.

We’re extending MissionOps so a scientist could request a close-up, send a rover to scout the outcrop, and use the returned image to decide whether to redirect the crew. Our goal is to help teams choose which rovers and instruments to send, and where an astronaut’s judgment is worth the crew time, payload mass, and mission cost.
details:
We’re building MissionOps to help Mars exploration teams decide where to send a rover and which sites are worth an astronaut’s time. We started with Jezero Crater, where a scientist planning a field visit can use something we already have: photos taken by Perseverance from the ground.

Our prototype brings NASA orbital imagery, USGS geology maps, and Perseverance’s observations into one browser. A scientist can pick a rock outcrop, see what the rover photographed nearby, and plan a round trip from base. In our demo, a 15.8 km route takes an estimated 5 hours and 27 minutes on foot. An hour at the site brings the outing to nearly six and a half hours. If the crew had six hours to get back to base, a one-hour stop at the outcrop would put it 27 minutes over time. The planners could shorten the stop or choose a closer target.

Getting the maps to line up was one of the harder parts. The geology overlay was off by 150–240 metres in places, enough to put a target on the wrong side of an outcrop. We corrected those offsets and matched rover panoramas to the crater skyline. We built the map in JavaScript with Leaflet, processed the terrain in Python, and tested the route calculations with Node.js. The planner uses slope, suit mass, and published walking models to estimate travel time and energy. Its 20-metre grid can still miss obstacles a crew would encounter on foot.

Next, we’re building a simulation where a scientist can request a rover close-up and revise the crew’s plan when the image comes back. We want teams rehearsing Mars missions on Earth to try the same science task two ways: send the crew directly, or send a rover first. Comparing what each approach reveals, how much crew time it takes, and what equipment it requires could help mission designers decide what is worth bringing to Mars in the first place.
